questions.q: If you have two numbers, 8,999 and 10,001, which one is larger without needing to look at individual digits?
questions.a: 10,001 is larger because it has 5 digits, while 8,999 only has 4. A wrong answer suggests the student is ignoring the total count of digits and only looking at the starting digit, which leads to thinking 8 is larger than 1.

questions.q: When comparing 5,672 and 5,627, why do we start looking at the thousands place instead of the ones place?
questions.a: We start from the left because the leftmost place value (thousands) carries the most weight in determining the total size of the number. A wrong answer shows a misunderstanding of place value, where the student might think all digits contribute equally to a number's magnitude.

questions.q: Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 2,345, 2,312, 2,399.
questions.a: The order is 2,312, 2,345, 2,399. We compare the thousands (all 2), then the hundreds (all 3), and finally the tens; since 1 < 4 < 9, the order is clear. A wrong answer indicates the student is not comparing digits systematically from left to right.

questions.q: If two numbers have the same digits in the thousands, hundreds, and tens places, what determines the larger number?
questions.a: The digit in the ones place determines the larger number. If a student says the numbers are equal, they have forgotten that every position is unique and contributes to the total value.

questions.q: Is it possible for a 4-digit number to be larger than a 5-digit number? Explain your reasoning.
questions.a: No, it is never possible because any 5-digit number starts at 10,000, which is already greater than the largest 4-digit number, 9,999. If a student thinks it is possible, they are likely confusing the value of individual digits with the total value of the number.

questions.q: Create a 4-digit number that is larger than 6,543 but smaller than 6,550.
questions.a: Any number like 6,544, 6,545, or 6,549 works. An incorrect answer usually shows the student doesn't understand the range between two values based on place-value progression.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Comparing numbers is the process of ______ the relative size of two or more values to identify which is greater or smaller.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are at the school library ______ for books with specific code numbers, like 4567 and 4589.
What is Comparing numbers? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Comparing numbers is the process of determining the relative size of two or more values to identify which is greater or smaller.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Comparing numbers?
questions.a: Students often compare the "size" of the numbers by looking only at the first digit they see (from left to right) without checking the number of digits first.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to order a set of four-digit to five-digit numbers from least to greatest and justify their choice by explaining the place-value comparison.
